lesson.title: Verbs of the Web: GET, POST, and the Rest
lesson.summary: An HTTP method tells the server what action to perform on the resource named in the request, and the choice of method carries real guarantees about safety and idempotency that well built clients and servers both rely on.
lesson.body:
The very first word in the request line you saw in the last chapter, GET, is the method, and it is not just a label. It is a promise about what kind of action the request performs, and both the client and the server are expected to honor that promise. HTTP defines several methods, and the ones worth knowing well are GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, and OPTIONS.

GET retrieves a resource, and it is expected to be safe, meaning it should not cause any side effect on the server, and idempotent, meaning sending the same GET five times has the same effect as sending it once: none. That is exactly what let the previous chapter's request simply fetch a page without changing anything on the server.

POST is the opposite kind of method. It is typically used to submit data to be processed, often creating a new resource in the process, such as placing a new order or posting a new comment. POST is neither safe nor idempotent: sending the same POST request twice can very reasonably create two separate orders instead of one.

PUT and PATCH both modify an existing resource, but they differ in an important way. PUT replaces the resource at a given URL entirely with whatever is in the request body, and it is idempotent, sending the exact same PUT five times in a row leaves the resource in the same final state as sending it once. PATCH applies a partial change rather than a full replacement, and it is not guaranteed to be idempotent, since a patch that means something like increment this counter by one produces a different result every time it is applied.

DELETE removes a resource, and like PUT it is idempotent in terms of end state: after the first DELETE the resource is gone, and every DELETE after that leaves it exactly as gone as before, even though the server will typically respond differently the second time, since there is no longer anything there to delete.

HEAD and OPTIONS are both about information rather than action. HEAD behaves exactly like GET but the server returns only the headers, no body, which lets a client cheaply check things like a resource's size or last modified date without downloading it. OPTIONS asks what the server actually supports for a given resource, which methods are allowed, and browsers use it automatically as a preflight check before sending certain cross origin requests, confirming the server permits them before the real request goes out.

A concrete pair shows the PUT versus PATCH distinction clearly. Sending PUT /users/42 with a complete JSON representation of the user replaces user 42's entire record with exactly what was sent, dropping anything not included. Sending PATCH /users/42 with just {"email": "new@example.com"} changes only the email field and leaves the rest of user 42's record untouched, which is the whole reason PATCH exists alongside PUT.
